newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban try to keep supply line to force in north.
newsitem.headline: Taleban try to keep supply line to force in north.

text.p: Opposition forces launched a fresh attack on Saturday on the Taleban militia around the town of Jabal-os-Siraj, astride the main highway from Kabul to northern Afghanistan. The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) said guerrillas commanded by Ahmad Shah Masood were trying to cut the vital road to isolate Taleban fighters further north.

A Taleban spokesman, Wakil Ahmad, told AIP that no ground had changed hands in the latest fighting, in which the two sides were pounding each other with artillery and rockets. Masood's forces broke out of his Panjsher Valley stronghold on Friday to capture the towns of Golbahar and Jabal-os-Siraj, but the Taleban said they had later retaken Jabal-os-Siraj.
No independent account of the clashes was available.
The Taleban must keep control of the highway to supply about 3,000 fighters sent north earlier in the week and now based in the town of Pul-i-Khumri, 160 km (100 miles) north of Kabul.

Ahmad said the Taleban had repulsed an attack by opposition forces near the town of Aibak, in Samangan province, 90 km (56 miles) north of Pul-i-Khumri, early on Saturday, killing 24 fighters, capturing 16 and destroying two ammunition trucks. He gave no figure for Taleban casualties.

The Taleban suffered a major setback on Wednesday when they were pushed out of the northern capital Mazar-i-Sharif by ethnic Uzbek and Shi'ite Moslem forces, only four days after they had entered it in a now-defunct alliance with the Uzbeks.

AIP said the Taleban were gathering thousands of fighters to reinforce their embattled frontlines. It said Islamic religious schools in neighbouring Pakistan had closed to allow 8,000 students to cross into Afghanistan to join the Taleban.

Pul-i-Khumri was quiet on Saturday, despite the Taleban's apparently precarious position there. Fighters were going around asking relief agencies to lend them their vehicles for a week. The Taleban are still reeling from their bloody defeat in Mazar-i-Sharif, the former stronghold of opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who was driven into exile in Turkey a week ago by his deputy, Gene ral Abdul Malik. Malik's troops captured several Taleban leaders in Mazar-i-Sharif, including their foreign minister, Mullah Mohammed Ghous, and military chief in the north, Mullah Abdul Razzak. Ahmad said he believed the two men were still alive.

Pakistan formally recognised the Taleban government in Kabul the day before the debacle in Mazar-i-Sharif. The Taleban still control more than two thirds of Afghanistan and enjoy widespread popular support in their ethnic Pashtun heartlands in the south.
